theme_scores.theme: Rebalancing the market via a fee ban
theme_scores.justification: The theme itself is pure assertion ('landlords will be able to shop around...'); the only relevant evidence elsewhere is Scotland's increase in letting-agent numbers 'indicating that the sector has become more competitive' (Ref 16), which is never explicitly tied back to this claim.

The 2016 Client Money Protection call for evidence is described ('stakeholders were asked whether the requirements have been effective', 'the majority of responses welcomed... but said that they are not sufficient') but without respondent numbers or a citation, so it stops at level 1.

theme_scores.theme: Scottish precedent as evidence for the ban
theme_scores.justification: Named, cited evidence (Ref 16: Shelter/Rettie/BDRC, Companies House, the '17%' and '56%' findings) is used and the document itself flags limits, noting the rent-rise finding is 'inconclusive' and that it is 'difficult to directly compare the English and Scottish markets'.

theme_scores.theme: Likely but acceptable pass-through to rents
theme_scores.justification: The claim is directly backed by the same cited Scottish evidence ('agents... are unlikely to pass the full costs of the fees onto landlords', Ref 16), with the document explicitly acknowledging uncertainty over how much of the Scottish rent rise is attributable to the fee ban.

theme_scores.theme: Scope and definition of the fee ban
theme_scores.justification: Describes the proposed scope of the ban with no evidence offered for why these particular boundaries were chosen.

theme_scores.theme: Benefits to tenants and social outcomes
theme_scores.justification: Asserts social benefits (reduced homelessness, easier saving for a deposit) without any data or research cited.

theme_scores.theme: Agent business model adjustment and deposit caps
theme_scores.justification: States rising deposit levels and likely business model changes as fact with no supporting figures or source.
A bare factual statement about regulatory status with no evidence attached.
States the proposal to introduce a regulatory framework with no evidence given for it.

reasoning: The four core themes vary sharply in evidential strength. 'Rebalancing the market' and 'Insufficiency of existing transparency regulation' both sit at level 1: the former offers no cited evidence at all beyond vague, unconnected references to Scottish competitiveness data, while the latter draws on the department's own 2016 Client Money Protection call for evidence ('the majority of responses welcomed... but said that they are not sufficient', 'many respondents said they have seen no evidence') but never says how many responded or gives a citation. By contrast, 'Scottish precedent' and 'Likely but acceptable pass-through to rents' both reach level 3: they rely on named, cited sources (Ref 16 - Shelter, Rettie, BDRC, Companies House) with concrete statistics ('17% of agencies claim to have increased fees', '56% of private tenants agreed'), and the document itself weighs the evidence, admitting the rent-rise link is 'inconclusive' and that it is 'difficult to directly compare the English and Scottish markets'. The mean of (1, 1, 3, 3) is 2.0, giving a section score of 2. The strongest counter-example is theme one, whose central mechanism (agents redirecting competitive effort toward landlords) is argued purely by assertion with no linked evidence. To reach level 3 overall, the weaker themes would need named, cited evidence - ideally with respondent numbers for the 2016 call for evidence - explicitly linked to the claimed mechanisms, and an acknowledgment of their own uncertainties as is done for the Scottish evidence.
